model_note.S:
cc: Brief spinning episodes when turning in bed

HPI: 24 yo m. Patient reports: It began 3 days ago. It feels like the room spins around me. There is no radiating pain. It is spinning rather than feeling faint. Each episode lasts about 20 seconds. It only happens with certain head movements; I feel well between spells. It first happened rolling onto my right side in bed. Keeping my head still stops it. Rolling right or looking up brings it on. I have avoided those movements. I have never had this before. Turning my head causes brief spinning. I feel briefly nauseated during a spell.

Patient perspective: I think I might be having a stroke.

PMH: No stroke, migraine or cervical spine disease.

PSH: No surgeries or admissions.

Meds: No daily medicines or sedatives.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. One alcoholic drink weekly. No recreational drugs. School administrator; lives with wife.

FH: Mother has hypertension; father had diabetes; one healthy sister.

ROS: Neurologic - Reports vertigo. Denies focal weakness. Denies diplopia. Gastrointestinal - Reports nausea. Denies vomiting. Denies abdominal pain. Cardiovascular - Denies syncope. Denies palpitations. Denies chest pain.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.2 F oral, P 76 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert and comfortable with head still.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Neuro: Face symmetric; speech clear; tongue midline. Strength 5/5 in both arms and legs. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin accurate bilaterally. Walks independently with stable gait between episodes. Right Dix–Hallpike after suitability review elicits brief vertigo and transient upbeating torsional nystagmus after a short latency. Left Dix–Hallpike after suitability review does not elicit vertigo or nystagmus.

Osteopathic: C1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Assess neurologic red flags and cervical suitability, then perform a trained positional assessment; discuss canalith repositioning by a trained clinician if findings support posterior-canal BPPV; educate on temporary fall/driving precautions while symptomatic and arrange reassessment within 1 month; seek urgent care for persistent vertigo with new focal deficits or inability to walk.

2. Escalate immediately for acute focal deficits, severe gait impairment or a concerning persistent syndrome; obtain stroke-team evaluation and appropriate imaging; educate the patient about urgent neurologic warning signs; do not use a normal basic examination or an untrained HINTS assessment to exclude stroke.

3. Clarify whether vertigo is continuous for days rather than brief triggered spells; assess hearing and neurologic findings and arrange clinician evaluation; explain why the current time course is less typical for neuritis. Arrange reassessment if symptoms become persistent, hearing changes develop, or function worsens; persistent symptoms warrant a focused hearing and vestibular evaluation after urgent central causes have been considered.

model_note.S:
cc: Brief spinning episodes when turning in bed

HPI: 24 yo m. Patient reports: It began 6 days ago. It feels like the room spins around me. There is no radiating pain. It is spinning rather than feeling faint. Each episode lasts about 20 seconds. It only happens with certain head movements; I feel well between spells. It first happened rolling onto my right side in bed. Keeping my head still stops it. Rolling right or looking up brings it on. I have avoided those movements. I have never had this before. Turning my head causes brief spinning. I feel briefly nauseated during a spell.

Patient perspective: I think I might be having a stroke.

PMH: No stroke, migraine or cervical spine disease.

PSH: No surgeries or admissions.

Meds: No daily medicines or sedatives.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. One alcoholic drink weekly. No recreational drugs. School administrator; lives with wife.

FH: Mother has hypertension; father had diabetes; one healthy sister.

ROS: Neurologic - Reports vertigo. Denies focal weakness. Denies diplopia. Gastrointestinal - Reports nausea. Denies vomiting. Denies abdominal pain. Cardiovascular - Denies syncope. Denies palpitations. Denies chest pain.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.2 F oral, P 76 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert and comfortable with head still.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Neuro: Face symmetric; speech clear; tongue midline. Strength 5/5 in both arms and legs. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin accurate bilaterally. Walks independently with stable gait between episodes. Right Dix–Hallpike after suitability review elicits brief vertigo and transient upbeating torsional nystagmus after a short latency. Left Dix–Hallpike after suitability review does not elicit vertigo or nystagmus.

Osteopathic: C1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Assess neurologic red flags and cervical suitability, then perform a trained positional assessment; discuss canalith repositioning by a trained clinician if findings support posterior-canal BPPV; educate on temporary fall/driving precautions while symptomatic and arrange reassessment within 1 month; seek urgent care for persistent vertigo with new focal deficits or inability to walk.

2. Escalate immediately for acute focal deficits, severe gait impairment or a concerning persistent syndrome; obtain stroke-team evaluation and appropriate imaging; educate the patient about urgent neurologic warning signs; do not use a normal basic examination or an untrained HINTS assessment to exclude stroke.

3. Clarify whether vertigo is continuous for days rather than brief triggered spells; assess hearing and neurologic findings and arrange clinician evaluation; explain why the current time course is less typical for neuritis. Arrange reassessment if symptoms become persistent, hearing changes develop, or function worsens; persistent symptoms warrant a focused hearing and vestibular evaluation after urgent central causes have been considered.

model_note.S:
cc: Brief spinning episodes when turning in bed

HPI: 24 yo m. Patient reports: It began 3 days ago. It feels like the room spins around me. There is no radiating pain. It is spinning rather than feeling faint. Each episode lasts about 20 seconds. It only happens with certain head movements; I feel well between spells. It first happened rolling onto my right side in bed. Keeping my head still stops it. Rolling right or looking up brings it on. I have avoided those movements. I have never had this before. Turning my head causes brief spinning. I feel briefly nauseated during a spell.

Patient perspective: I think I might be having a stroke.

PMH: No stroke, migraine or cervical spine disease.

PSH: No surgeries or admissions.

Meds: No daily medicines or sedatives.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. One alcoholic drink weekly. No recreational drugs. School administrator; lives with wife.

FH: Mother has hypertension; father had diabetes; one healthy sister.

ROS: Neurologic - Reports vertigo. Denies focal weakness. Denies diplopia. Gastrointestinal - Reports nausea. Denies vomiting. Denies abdominal pain. Cardiovascular - Denies syncope. Denies palpitations. Denies chest pain.

Patient concern: I am afraid to lie back because I know the spinning will start.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.2 F oral, P 76 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert and comfortable with head still.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Neuro: Face symmetric; speech clear; tongue midline. Strength 5/5 in both arms and legs. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin accurate bilaterally. Walks independently with stable gait between episodes. Right Dix–Hallpike after suitability review elicits brief vertigo and transient upbeating torsional nystagmus after a short latency. Left Dix–Hallpike after suitability review does not elicit vertigo or nystagmus.

Osteopathic: C1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Assess neurologic red flags and cervical suitability, then perform a trained positional assessment; discuss canalith repositioning by a trained clinician if findings support posterior-canal BPPV; educate on temporary fall/driving precautions while symptomatic and arrange reassessment within 1 month; seek urgent care for persistent vertigo with new focal deficits or inability to walk. Explain the brief expected sensation, request consent, agree on a stop signal and support the patient physically.

2. Escalate immediately for acute focal deficits, severe gait impairment or a concerning persistent syndrome; obtain stroke-team evaluation and appropriate imaging; educate the patient about urgent neurologic warning signs; do not use a normal basic examination or an untrained HINTS assessment to exclude stroke.

3. Clarify whether vertigo is continuous for days rather than brief triggered spells; assess hearing and neurologic findings and arrange clinician evaluation; explain why the current time course is less typical for neuritis. Arrange reassessment if symptoms become persistent, hearing changes develop, or function worsens; persistent symptoms warrant a focused hearing and vestibular evaluation after urgent central causes have been considered.
